metrics.name: Relative Denitrification Potential
metrics.metricStatement: Denitrification removes nitrate by converting it to nitrogen gases under anoxic, carbon‑rich, and saturated conditions. Connected floodplains and wetlands are key hotspots for this process and can substantially reduce nitrate export from watersheds.

likertCriteria.criteria: Strong potential with frequent seasonal saturation
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Connected floodplain wetlands with hydric soils and backwater pockets.

likertCriteria.criteria: Moderate potential
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Some wet pockets. Channel partly disconnected from floodplain.

likertCriteria.criteria: Low potential
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Limited wetland area. Bankfull rarely overtops.

likertCriteria.criteria: Negligible potential
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: No wetlands. Floodplain ditched or tile drained.

metrics.name: Water Clarity / Turbidity
metrics.metricStatement: Turbidity reduces sunlight, which is needed for primary production, and can clog gills. Suspended sediments also carry nutrients and metals on particle surfaces that can worsen water‑quality problems.

likertCriteria.criteria: Mostly clear or only slightly cloudy at baseflow.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Water is clear at baseflow and similar to a local reference reach. Bottom is visible at knee depth.

likertCriteria.criteria: Slight turbidity or color that is short-lived.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Slight yellow-brown tint after storms that clears within a day.

likertCriteria.criteria: Persistent cloudiness at baseflow.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Cloudy water persists during baseflow. Fine sediment coats substrate.

likertCriteria.criteria: Persistently muddy or sheen present.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Chronically muddy water. Visible oily sheen or scum in slack water.

metrics.name: Dissolved Oxygen (rapid)
metrics.metricStatement: Dissolved oxygen (DO) supports respiration for fish and invertebrates. Low DO can cause acute stress, avoidance, and fish kills.

likertCriteria.criteria: > 6 mg/L consistently.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: DO readings consistently above 6 mg/L. No recorded night-time dips.

likertCriteria.criteria: 5–6 mg/L borderline.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: DO commonly 5–6 mg/L in late summer.

likertCriteria.criteria: 3–5 mg/L frequent stress.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Night minima 3–5 mg/L during warm periods.

likertCriteria.criteria: < 3 mg/L dangerously low.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: DO dips below 3 mg/L and fish stress observed.

metrics.name: Pollutants
metrics.metricStatement: Pollution in water and floodplain soils, including metals, hydrocarbons, pesticides, and emerging contaminants, can cause stress or mortality and can build up in food webs. Contaminated or fill‑dominated floodplain soils can leach pollutants to the channel and reduce riparian filtration and bank stability.

likertCriteria.criteria: No visible contamination indicators or known exceedances.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: No oily sheen, staining, or chemical odor. Soils appear natural and intact. No impairment listings.

likertCriteria.criteria: Minor localized inputs or mild odor only.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Occasional faint odor near a storm outfall or small dump pile on the floodplain.

likertCriteria.criteria: Recognized contamination risk or known moderate contamination.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Stained soils, debris, or chemical odor near developed or industrial areas. Located downstream of a listed contaminated site.

likertCriteria.criteria: Severe or chronic contamination.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Strong odor, visible seepage, recurring sheen, or known hazardous site on the floodplain. Fish kill reports on record.

metrics.name: pH & Specific Conductivity (rapid)
metrics.metricStatement: pH controls metal solubility and toxicity. Specific conductivity indicates ionic strength from dissolved salts. Values outside typical ranges often signal mine drainage, road salt, brines, or wastewater influence and can impair aquatic communities.

likertCriteria.criteria: pH ~6.5–8.5 and cond. < 500 µS/cm typical.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: pH 7.4. Specific conductance 250 µS/cm.

likertCriteria.criteria: Slightly off-range or mild elevation.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: pH 6.3 or 8.7 with otherwise stable chemistry.

likertCriteria.criteria: Marked deviation or 800–1500 µS/cm.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: pH 5.8 or 9.2. Conductivity ~1000 µS/cm.

likertCriteria.criteria: Extreme pH or very high conductance.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: pH 4.8 or 10.2. Conductivity > 2000 µS/cm.

metrics.name: Bank & Floodplain Soil Condition
metrics.metricStatement: Bank & Floodplain Soil Condition

likertCriteria.criteria: Natural soils. No contamination indicators.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Intact native soils and vegetation. No odors or staining.

likertCriteria.criteria: Minor dumping or localized inputs.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Small dump pile or localized manure near a crossing.

likertCriteria.criteria: Known moderate contamination.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Stained soils and debris on banks near former industrial area.

likertCriteria.criteria: Highly contaminated soils.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Strong petroleum odor, visible seepage, or listed hazardous site on the floodplain.

metrics.name: In-Stream Habitat Complexity
metrics.metricStatement: This metric captures the variety and arrangement of habitat units such as riffles, runs, pools, and cover elements. Greater diversity of units increases niche space and supports higher productivity and resilience.

likertCriteria.criteria: Multiple habitat types well represented.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Riffles, runs, pools, and large wood recur across the reach.

likertCriteria.criteria: Some variety but missing key elements.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Riffle and run common. Pools intermittent. Sparse cover.

likertCriteria.criteria: Mostly uniform. Only 1–2 distinct features.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Long uniform glide or sand bed with occasional shallow run.

likertCriteria.criteria: Very uniform channel. Limited structural diversity.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Straight, entrenched, uniform channel with little cover.

metrics.name: Overhanging Vegetation
metrics.metricStatement: Overhanging vegetation provides cover from predators and high velocities. They can also create shaded microhabitats important for many fishes and amphibians.

likertCriteria.criteria: About 50% or more of banks provide overhanging cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Thick root mats and overhanging shrubs along outside bends.

likertCriteria.criteria: About 25–50% cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Intermittent and low branches in meanders.

likertCriteria.criteria: About 10–25% cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Short isolated pockets with overhanging vegetation.

likertCriteria.criteria: <10% cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Little to no overhanging vegetation.

metrics.name: Aquatic Invertebrate Habitat
metrics.metricStatement: Stable substrates such as cobble, coarse wood, and persistent leaf packs provide attachment points and refuges for invertebrates, including sensitive mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies (EPT) that underpin food webs. A mix of substrate sizes and small organic pockets creates small‑scale velocity and shelter contrasts that support diverse invertebrates and foraging fishes. Expectations should reflect local reference conditions. In some ephemeral or bedrock channels, more uniform substrates can be natural.

likertCriteria.criteria: Multiple stable substrates and organic cover supporting diverse invertebrates.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Stable cobble riffles with gravel pockets, root wads, leaf packs, and scattered wood.

likertCriteria.criteria: Some substrate variety but partly limited by fines.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Cobble and gravel with some roots or wood. Fines cover parts of the bed.

likertCriteria.criteria: Limited stable substrate and few microhabitats.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Mostly mobile sand or silt with little wood or leaf packs.

likertCriteria.criteria: Very poor substrate variety and minimal invertebrate habitat.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Uniform sand, silt, or bedrock. No wood, leaf packs, or root structure.

metrics.name: Lateral and Off-Channel Habitats
metrics.metricStatement: Side channels, connected backwaters, and seasonally active floodplain wetlands provide refuge during high flows, warm periods, and winter conditions. They also offer spawning and rearing areas and increase survival during disturbances.

likertCriteria.criteria: Well connected off-channel areas offering refuge and spawning.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Side channels and backwaters connect during seasonal highs. Fish and amphibian use observed.

likertCriteria.criteria: Some partial connection.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: One or two backwaters with partial seasonal connection.

likertCriteria.criteria: Rare or only ephemeral off-channel usage.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Small depressions connect only during rare floods.

likertCriteria.criteria: No side channels or backwaters remain.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Levees or berms isolate the channel from the floodplain.

metrics.name: Fish habitat
metrics.metricStatement: Successful reproduction is supported by low embeddedness and good spawning habitat. Fish spawning requires clean, well‑sorted gravel or other appropriate materials where that is the reference condition. Excess fine sediment fills spaces between gravels, reduces oxygen delivery to eggs, and lowers embryo survival. Juveniles need shallow, low‑velocity margins with cover from wood, undercuts, or vegetation. These areas help them avoid displacement and predators and improve survival during high flows and heat. Where vegetation or other substrates are the normal spawning medium for native fauna, judge condition against that reference.

likertCriteria.criteria: Embeddedness 0–25 percent; over 40 percent shallow, low-velocity cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Clean gravels with open spaces and many shallow pockets, wood, and vegetation.

likertCriteria.criteria: Embeddedness 25–50 percent; about 20–40 percent shallow, low-velocity cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Light sand on riffles; scattered wood and bank cover.

likertCriteria.criteria: Embeddedness 50–75 percent; about 5–20 percent shallow, low-velocity cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Gravels embedded with silt; few bank pockets or calm margins.

likertCriteria.criteria: Embeddedness ≥75 percent; less than 5 percent shallow, low-velocity cover.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Bed mostly sand or silt; no pockets or structural cover.

metrics.name: Aquatic Invertebrate Community
metrics.metricStatement: Sensitive aquatic insects such as mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies provide food for fishes and amphibians and could be used as indicators of habitat and water quality conditions that support populations.

likertCriteria.criteria: All three EPT orders present with multiple taxa.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies found in kick sample.

likertCriteria.criteria: Two EPT orders present.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Two of three EPT orders present.

likertCriteria.criteria: One EPT order present.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Only one EPT order present.

likertCriteria.criteria: Zero EPT orders present.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: No EPT. Mostly tolerant midges and worms.

metrics.name: Fish Presence
metrics.metricStatement: A healthy fish assemblage includes multiple native species with a range of body sizes that reflect successful growth and survival. Regular appearance of young-of-year across edge habitats, riffles, and backwaters signals that spawning, incubation, and early juvenile survival are functioning. Dominance by only a few tolerant species, absence of natives, or a lack of young-of-year signals stressors that limit population support.

likertCriteria.criteria: Multiple native species with broad size classes.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Several native species across many sizes.

likertCriteria.criteria: Few natives with partial size classes.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Two to three natives; sizes limited.

likertCriteria.criteria: One to two tolerant species dominate.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Only tolerant species present in low numbers.

likertCriteria.criteria: Absent or only non-native species present.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: No fish detected where expected.

metrics.name: Amphibian and Crayfish Presence
metrics.metricStatement: Amphibians and crayfishes are sensitive to changes in hydrology, temperature, and habitat complexity. Their presence and diversity complement fish and macroinvertebrate indicators, especially in small streams.

likertCriteria.criteria: Presence aligns with reference expectations.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Multiple frogs, salamanders, and crayfish observed.

likertCriteria.criteria: Limited presence.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: A few individuals observed.

likertCriteria.criteria: Rare occurrence.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: One or two sightings only.

likertCriteria.criteria: Absent where historically expected.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: None detected during suitable season.

metrics.name: Native and non-native species
metrics.metricStatement: Communities dominated by native fish and invertebrates that reflect historical or regional reference conditions indicate that habitats and water quality are sufficient to support expected biodiversity. Loss of sensitive native species, increases in tolerant generalists, and a growing share of non-native or invasive taxa signal stress, biotic homogenization, and reduced ecological resilience Non-native and invasive are not equivalent. Where possible, base the score on the percent of invasive taxa with a clear definition, since some non-native species are common even in otherwise functional systems. Because observed species vary with sampling timing and location, this metric is most reliable when based on a compiled multi-year or multi-site record rather than a single visit..

likertCriteria.criteria: Native community matches reference. Non natives rare and low abundance.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Native fish and invertebrates common. Very few non natives seen.

likertCriteria.criteria: Minor native loss. Non natives present but natives still dominant.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Most natives present. Some sensitive species missing.

likertCriteria.criteria: Noticeable native decline. Non natives common or co-dominant.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Many sensitive natives gone. Non natives frequent.

likertCriteria.criteria: Natives rare or absent. Community dominated by tolerant or invasive taxa.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Only tolerant or non native species observed.

metrics.name: Species richness, composition and abundance
metrics.metricStatement: Species richness and community composition reflect overall habitat quality and environmental condition. A healthy stream supports multiple major macroinvertebrate groups, including sensitive EPT taxa, along with a balanced mix of functional feeding groups that indicate a well-organized food web. High richness and a diverse set of guilds suggest intact habitat and water quality. Declines in richness, dominance by tolerant taxa, or simplified feeding groups often signal stress and reduced ecological integrity.

likertCriteria.criteria: High richness. Balanced feeding groups. Good index score.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Many species across several feeding groups.

likertCriteria.criteria: Moderate richness. Some imbalance in feeding groups.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Several species present. Some groups missing.

likertCriteria.criteria: Low richness. Dominance by tolerant taxa or single group.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Few species. One or two groups dominate.

likertCriteria.criteria: Extremely low richness and diversity. Poor index score.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Very few species. Mostly tolerant taxa.

metrics.name: Riparian communities
metrics.metricStatement: Healthy riparian communities include the expected mix of native trees, shrubs, and groundcover that provide shade, organic matter, wood, bank stability, and habitat. Communities that resemble local reference conditions support better biological integrity by moderating temperature, filtering runoff, and supplying food and cover for aquatic and terrestrial species. Native riparian communities with multiple vegetation layers also support keystone species such as beaver, mussels, and crayfish where they are naturally expected.

likertCriteria.criteria: Wide, intact native corridor with minimal invasives.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Continuous native trees, shrubs, and groundcover.

likertCriteria.criteria: Moderate width and structure. Some invasive patches present.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Mostly vegetated corridor with some gaps.

likertCriteria.criteria: Narrow corridor. Fragmented native cover with common invasives.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Thin or patchy vegetation along banks.

likertCriteria.criteria: Corridor very narrow or absent. Native plants largely missing.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Little native vegetation. Banks mostly lawn or invasives.

desktopSource.label: EPA EnviroAtlas riparian; StreamCat; NLCD

metrics.name: Keystone species
metrics.metricStatement: Keystone species such as beaver, freshwater mussels, and large crayfish play an outsized role in maintaining stream health. Beaver create off-channel habitat, increase hydraulic complexity, and help buffer baseflow. Mussels, crayfish, and similar taxa filter water, stabilize food webs, and engineer habitat structure. Healthy populations indicate strong ecological integrity, while absence where historically expected or severe overabundance that disrupts connectivity are warning signs of degradation Confirming mussels, crayfish, or similar taxa often requires permits, trained surveyors, and specific methods, so where those are not available, assess keystone presence when feasible and record a confidence flag rather than a definitive absence..

likertCriteria.criteria: Expected keystone taxa widespread. No invasive dominance.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Beaver, mussels, or crayfish common where expected.

likertCriteria.criteria: At least one keystone taxon present but limited distribution.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Some keystone species present but patchy.

likertCriteria.criteria: Keystone taxa rare compared to reference or historical levels.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Keystone species observed only in small numbers.

likertCriteria.criteria: No keystone taxa present. Strong invasive dominance.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Expected keystone species absent. Invasives common.

metrics.name: Upstream and Downstream Barriers
metrics.metricStatement: This metric captures how dams, weirs, grade controls, and natural drops restrict longitudinal movement. Fewer or smaller barriers mean more habitat is connected. This improves dispersal, gene flow, and recolonization after floods, droughts, or spills.

likertCriteria.criteria: 80–100% of habitat accessible. No major barriers.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: No dams or weirs within the connected corridor. Only small natural steps that fish pass at typical flows.

likertCriteria.criteria: About 50–80% accessible.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: One small low-head structure downstream with partial passage at moderate flows.

likertCriteria.criteria: About 20–50% accessible.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Several small barriers in series restrict movement across subreaches.

likertCriteria.criteria: <20% accessible due to big dams or multiple blockages.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Large regulating dam close to the reach with multiple downstream grade controls.

desktopSource.label: National Aquatic Barrier Inventory (USFWS/TNC) + USACE NID

metrics.name: Culvert and Road-Crossing Passability
metrics.metricStatement: This metric evaluates whether stream–road crossings allow aquatic organisms and drift to pass at a wide range of flows. Perched outlets, excessive slopes, and smooth barrel conditions can block passage and fragment habitat, even in otherwise connected reaches.

likertCriteria.criteria: 80–100% stream continuity at crossings.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Crossings are embedded and aligned with natural bed. No outlet drops.

likertCriteria.criteria: About 50–80% passable.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Most crossings passable. A few show minor outlet drops or smooth barrels.

likertCriteria.criteria: About 20–50% passable.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Several perched culverts and steep barrels concentrate flow and block passage.

likertCriteria.criteria: <20% passable. Multiple perched culverts hamper movement.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Many perched pipes and long smooth boxes with no bed material.

metrics.name: Lateral Connectivity for Riparian Fauna
metrics.metricStatement: This metric considers whether levees, berms, walls, or continuous revetment trap semi‑aquatic fauna in the channel or prevent movement across the floodplain. Open lateral corridors allow amphibians, reptiles, mammals, and insects to move between wetlands, backwaters, and riparian cover for feeding, breeding, and refuge.

likertCriteria.criteria: No major levees or walls. Free lateral movement for semiaquatic fauna.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Banks are free of continuous levees or walls. Side channels and backwaters are accessible.

likertCriteria.criteria: Some partial barriers but still some access.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Short levee segments occur, but frequent gaps allow movement to wetlands.

likertCriteria.criteria: Large levees hamper movement in many areas.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Long levees or riprapped banks on one side limit access to the floodplain in many places.

likertCriteria.criteria: Heavily walled or leveed corridor. Minimal lateral connectivity.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Both banks armored or walled for long distances. Few or no access points.

metrics.name: Dewatered or Intermittent Segments
metrics.metricStatement: This metric identifies artificial dry‑downs and chronic disconnections that strand biota and break longitudinal pathways. Persistent or seasonal dewatering prevents movement among habitats and can cause repeated local extirpations.

likertCriteria.criteria: No artificial dryness. Natural connectivity is maintained.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Continuous wetted channel during the expected season. No artificial withdrawals noted.

likertCriteria.criteria: Minor dryness in small segments.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Short dry patches appear during late season but reconnect after small rains.

likertCriteria.criteria: Notable dryness or disconnection in key reaches.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Long dry segments form in critical habitat areas during the growing season.

likertCriteria.criteria: Chronic or large-scale dewatering. Major fragmentation.
likertCriteria.exampleObservation: Reaches are chronically dewatered or disconnected for long periods due to withdrawals or diversions.
